title: World Food Detective
goal: Your kid picks the dish people here eat most and investigates it like a detective. They taste it in a few places, trace where each ingredient comes from, learn to make it from a local cook, then make it again somewhere else and work out why it doesn't taste quite the same.
need: A place you're staying long enough to eat the same dish more than once
A local cook, a cooking class or a market stall willing to show you
A notebook for the food file
A kitchen to try it again, here or back home

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Order the same dish again, even when everyone wants something new: the second and third plates are where the detective work happens. Ask the person who made it one question each time. At the class, stand right beside them at anything hot, and let the cook do the correcting.

plan.what: Find the dish, then taste it in a few places (Steps 1 and 2).

plan.when: At the market or the grinder

plan.what: Learn it from a local cook (Step 4).

troubleshoot.a: Ask the person who sells it. Many cooks will let a curious kid watch for a few minutes at a quiet time.
Let them investigate it without eating it first: the smell, the ingredients, who orders it. Curiosity usually wins by the second visit.

troubleshoot.q: The family has allergies or diets
troubleshoot.a: Pick a dish everyone can eat, or investigate one dish while eating another.

lesson.text: A dish is a set of answers about a place: what grows here, how people cook, and what they eat together. You find the answers by tasting, asking and making it yourself.

model.line: We ate them at the pupusería a few times before the class.
The corn is ground into masa on the only grinder around, right in the restaurant.
Fillings of cheese, beans and chicharrón, with curtido and salsa on the side.
Made at home in the spring, they didn't taste the same at all.

lesson.modelNote: 'Just stuffed tortillas' missed everything that made them taste like El Salvador. Watching the corn become masa on the village's only grinder, and failing to copy them at home, showed how much the place was part of the recipe.

steps.title: Find the dish
steps.why: Every place has a dish people eat without thinking, and that's the one worth investigating.
steps.kid: Your kid finds out which dish people here eat most, using the Find the dish card in the Food Detective Toolkit at the end of the guide: what's on every menu, what locals order, what a cook says is the traditional meal. They read a little about it before they taste it.
steps.you: Ask 'What do people here eat most often?' rather than 'What's famous?' Help them read about it, and keep a list of where it's sold.
ask: What do you think is in it?
Why might people here eat it so often?
steps.tip: Reading about the dish before you go makes the first bite feel like a discovery, not just dinner.

levels.explore: Spot one dish you see everywhere, and draw what you think is inside.
levels.develop: Find the traditional dish and three facts about it before you taste it.
levels.extend: Find out how long people here have eaten it, and what it was made with before.

steps.title: Taste it like a detective
steps.why: Tasting it in more than one place shows what stays the same and what each cook does differently.
steps.kid: Your kid tastes the dish in two or three places and fills in the Taste notes card each time: the texture, the flavour, the smell and what it comes with. They notice what's the same everywhere and what changes.
steps.you: Order it again, even when it's tempting to try something new. Ask 'What's different about this one?' and let them find words for it.
ask: What's the same in every one you've tried?
Which was your favourite, and why?
steps.tip: Watch what locals add to it at the table. That's often part of the dish too.

levels.explore: Taste it once, and say one word for how it feels and one for how it tastes.
levels.develop: Taste it in two places, fill in the Taste notes, and pick a favourite.
levels.extend: Taste it in three places, and work out what one cook does that the others don't.

steps.title: Trace the ingredients
steps.why: Following an ingredient back to where it comes from turns a meal into geography.
steps.kid: Your kid lists every ingredient and traces as many as they can, using the Trace it card: does it grow here, is it made by hand, where would you buy it, what does it cost? If they can, they see one ingredient being made, like corn ground into dough at a mill.
steps.you: Take them to the market, the mill or the shop where the ingredients are sold. Ask the seller, with them beside you, where it comes from. Keep them back from any grinding machine, and watch from where the owner says.
ask: What would be hardest to find back home?
steps.tip: Seeing one ingredient made from scratch, like corn becoming dough, is often the moment the whole dish makes sense.

levels.explore: Find two ingredients at a market, and say if they grow here.
levels.develop: Trace every ingredient: grown here, made here, or brought in.
levels.extend: Price the ingredients for one serving, and compare it with what the dish costs to buy.

steps.title: Learn it from a local cook
steps.why: A cook's hands know things no recipe writes down.
steps.kid: Your kid learns to make the dish from someone local: a cooking class, a cook at a stall or a host. They watch first, ask the questions on the Ask the cook card, then make it with their own hands, including what's served with it.
steps.you: Find the lesson and help with the asking. Stand right beside them at the griddle, and handle the knives yourself. Let the cook correct your kid, not you, and take photos of their hands at work.
ask: What's the one thing beginners always get wrong?
What do you put on the side, and why?
steps.tip: Ask the cook how they learned it. The answer is often a story about their family.

levels.explore: Watch the cook, then shape or fill one yourself.
levels.develop: Make the whole dish with the cook, side dishes included, and ask two questions.
levels.extend: Ask the cook what they'd change if they made it in another country, and write down why.

steps.title: Make it again and compare
steps.why: When the dish doesn't taste the same somewhere else, working out why is the best detective work of all.
steps.kid: Your kid makes the dish again in a new kitchen, here or back home, from the recipe they wrote. Then they compare it with the real thing and fill in My food file at the end of the guide: what was different, and why they think so.
steps.you: Shop for the ingredients with them, and let them find substitutes when the real ones aren't there. Taste it together and be honest.
ask: What tastes different, and what do you think caused it?
What would you need to make it taste like there?
steps.tip: It almost never tastes the same, and that's the point. The reasons are the place itself: the corn, the cook's hands, the griddle.

levels.explore: Help make it again, and say one thing that tastes different.
levels.develop: Make it from your recipe, then list what was different and why.
levels.extend: Change one thing, like the flour or the heat, and test whether it gets closer.

conclusion.headline: They tasted a place, and found out what made it taste that way.
conclusion.text: At your next meal out, hand the new plate to your kid first. Watch whether they smell it, ask what's in it or check what the next table added before they take a bite.
conclusion.celebrate: When they explain why their version tastes different, say: 'You worked out what the recipe couldn't bring with it. That's real detective work.'
extensions: Find a dish from this place that's eaten on one special day of the year, and find out why
Track down the same ingredient in three dishes here, and see how it changes
Cook the dish for family back home who has never tried it, and tell them its story
Compare the dish with one from home that's built the same way, and list what's different

signs: They ask what's in a dish before they decide if they like it
They want to see where ingredients are sold
They order something because locals do
makeItReal: Make the first meal in each new place a detective meal: your kid picks the everyday dish, orders it for the family and tells everyone one thing they found out about it before the first bite.

fromHome.text: Pupusas are the traditional meal in El Salvador, so we read about them before we went. We ate them at the pupusería a few times, then our Spanish school offered a cooking class. The restaurant had the only corn grinder in the area, so people came from all around to pay to grind their corn there. The kids saw it ground into masa, filled pupusas with cheese, beans and chicharrón, and made curtido and salsa to go with them. In the spring we tried making them at home. They didn't taste the same at all.
